notes.title: Start here: an expense tracker in four classes
notes.body:
This repo (named `src` on GitHub) is a terminal expense tracker in plain Java 17. You add expenses, list and filter them, and see totals; everything is kept in `data/expenses.txt`.

Four classes, one job each:

- **App.java** - the menu, the prompts, the table printing, and loading and saving around the menu loop.
- **ExpenseManager.java** - the rules: turning typed text into valid values, ids, filters and totals.
- **Expense.java** - one expense; its constructor refuses invalid values.
- **ExpenseFileStorage.java** - the tab-separated file, with escaping.

The README explains every method and walks through adding, filtering, totals and saving. Read it beside the code, and trust the code when they differ.

To try things, compile with `javac -d out src/expensetracker/*.java` and run `java -cp out expensetracker.App` in a scratch folder. Several questions here are about a hand-edited data file, so after your first run, open `data/expenses.txt` in an editor and look at exactly what was written.

readMore.why: One entry per method, then the add, filter, total and save flows.

notes.title: Concept: typed input and loaded data take different paths
notes.body:
An `Expense` can come into existence in two ways. Compare, field by field, what each path does to the values.

1. **Typed by the user.** `App.addExpenseFlow` collects raw strings and hands them to `ExpenseManager.addExpense`, which cleans and validates each one with helpers such as `parseAmount`, `normalizeCategory` and `parseDate`.
2. **Read from the file.** `ExpenseFileStorage.parseLine` converts the fields itself and calls the `Expense` constructor directly.

Make a table with one row per field (title, amount, category, date, note) and two columns, one per path. In each cell write what is done to the value: trimmed, re-cased, scale checked, sign checked, parsed, or nothing. Then look at the code that reads the values back out later: `getSpendingByCategory`, `getExpensesByCategory` and `App.formatAmount`. For each one, ask what it assumes about the values it receives, and whether both paths guarantee that.

Also find every `setScale` call in the project, note the rounding mode each one passes, and look up what that mode does when digits would have to be dropped.

excerpts.quote: `ExpenseManager` is the middle layer between the CLI and the stored data.

notes.title: Concept: a tab-separated file with escapes
notes.body:
Each expense is one line of six fields separated by tab characters: id, title, amount, category, date and note. The file starts with a `#` header comment. Because a title or note could itself contain a tab or a newline, `escape` rewrites those as two-character codes, and `splitPreservingEscapes` plus `unescape` undo it.

Trace a save and a load by hand:

- Write the exact line `toLine` produces for an expense, marking every tab.
- Follow `load` line by line: what is done to each line before it is split, which lines are skipped, and how the field count is checked.
- When `parseLine` throws, what does `load` do with that line, and what does it do with the lines after it?
- Find where and when `run()` saves. Write down where the saved list comes from, and compare it with what was in the file at start-up.

Then test your trace: run the app, add two expenses, exit, start again, and list.

excerpts.quote: The file format is a simple plain-text tab-separated format.

notes.title: Why 12.345 is refused instead of rounded
notes.body:
`parseAmount` calls `new BigDecimal(value).setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY)`. `UNNECESSARY` means "I promise no rounding is needed"; if digits would have to be dropped, it throws `ArithmeticException`. The catch turns that into **"Amount must use at most 2 decimal places."**, which `addExpenseFlow` prints after "Could not add expense: ".

- *Rounded half-up to 12.35*: that would need `RoundingMode.HALF_UP`.
- *Cut to 12.34*: that would need `RoundingMode.DOWN`.
- *Not a valid number*: 12.345 parses fine; that message is for `NumberFormatException`.

excerpts.quote: } catch (ArithmeticException ex) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must use at most 2 decimal places.");

notes.title: Why 12.340 is accepted as 12.34
notes.body:
`setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY)` only throws when reducing the scale would change the value. Removing a trailing zero does not: 12.340 and 12.34 are the same number. So the amount becomes **12.34** with scale 2, passes the sign check, and is saved with `toPlainString()` as 12.34.

- *Refused for three digits*: the check is on the value, not on how many digits were typed.
- *Stored as 12.340*: the scaled value is what the `Expense` holds and what `toLine` writes.
- *Refused for a trailing zero*: no rule looks at the typed text's last digit.

notes.title: How a typed category is normalised
notes.body:
`normalizeCategory` trims the text, splits it on `\s+` (any run of whitespace), and rebuilds it word by word: the first letter upper-cased, the rest lower-cased, single spaces between words. "  food   and DRINK " becomes **Food And Drink**.

- *food and DRINK*: that is only a trim; the method also re-cases every word.
- *FOOD AND DRINK*: only the first letter of each word is upper-cased.
- *Food and drink*: every word is treated alike, not only the first one.

notes.title: Why only the title error is shown
notes.body:
`addExpenseFlow` prompts for title, amount, category, date and note one after another, with no checks in between. Only then does it call `addExpense`, which validates in a fixed order: `requireText(title)`, then `parseAmount`, then `normalizeCategory`, then `parseDate`. The first failure throws, so the user sees **"Title cannot be blank."** after all five prompts.

- *Stops after the empty title*: `App.prompt` just reads a line; it never validates.
- *All four errors*: an exception ends `addExpense` at the first problem.
- *The amount error*: the title is checked before the amount.

excerpts.quote: String cleanTitle = requireText(title, "Title"); BigDecimal amount = parseAmount(amountText);

notes.title: Why a real-looking date gets a format error
notes.body:
`LocalDate.parse("2026-02-30")` checks that the day exists in that month and throws `DateTimeParseException` because February 2026 has no 30th. `parseDate` catches every `DateTimeParseException` and throws the same message, **"Date must use the format yyyy-MM-dd."**, even though the format was right. The message is misleading here, but that is what the code prints.

- *Moved to 2026-03-02 or 2026-02-28*: `LocalDate.parse` never adjusts an invalid date; it refuses it.
- *"February 2026 only has 28 days in it."*: no message that specific exists.

excerpts.quote: try { return LocalDate.parse(value); } catch (DateTimeParseException ex) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("Date must use the format yyyy-MM-dd.");

notes.title: Why 2026-3 is not accepted as a month
notes.body:
`YearMonth.parse` uses the ISO pattern with a two-digit month, so "2026-3" throws `DateTimeParseException`. `parseYearMonth` turns that into "Month must use the format yyyy-MM.", and `filterByMonthFlow` prints it after "Could not filter by month: ". **Nothing is listed.**

- *Lists March 2026*: that needs the input 2026-03.
- *"No expenses found."*: that is printed only after a successful parse with no matches.
- *Every 2026 expense*: there is no fallback to a year-only filter.

excerpts.quote: return YearMonth.parse(value); } catch (DateTimeParseException ex) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("Month must use the format yyyy-MM.");

notes.title: Why two spellings make two summary lines
notes.body:
Only typed categories pass through `normalizeCategory`. A record loaded by `parseLine` keeps the category text from the file exactly. `getSpendingByCategory` uses that text as the key of a `LinkedHashMap`, and map keys are case-sensitive, so "transport" and "Transport" are **two lines, totalled separately**, in the order first seen.

- *One line, Transport $6.50*: nothing compares categories ignoring case in the summary.
- *One line named after the first*: the second spelling is a different key, not a match.
- *Both shown as Transport*: the printed key is the stored text, unchanged.

excerpts.quote: String category = expense.getCategory(); BigDecimal currentTotal = totals.getOrDefault(category, BigDecimal.ZERO);

notes.title: Why the category filter finds both spellings
notes.body:
`getExpensesByCategory` first normalises the requested text, so TRANSPORT becomes Transport. It then compares each stored category with `equalsIgnoreCase`, which treats "transport" and "Transport" as equal. **Both expenses are listed.** Note the contrast with the summary, which keys a map by the exact text.

- *Neither*: the comparison is not exact.
- *Only Transport*: normalising the input alone would do that, but the comparison also ignores case.
- *Only transport*: same reason; both spellings match.

notes.title: Why a bad line is skipped and then lost
notes.body:
`load` wraps each `parseLine` call in its own `try`/`catch (IllegalArgumentException)`. A bad amount makes `parseLine` throw "Could not parse expense record.", `load` prints "Skipping invalid saved record on line N: ..." and continues, so the **other lines load**. The skipped line never reaches the manager. On exit, the `finally` block in `run()` saves `getAllExpenses()`, which rewrites the whole file, so the bad line **is dropped**.

- *Loading stops*: the catch is inside the loop.
- *Written back unchanged*: the save writes only what the manager holds.
- *Loaded as 0.00*: there is no default; the `Expense` constructor also refuses zero.

excerpts.quote: try { expenses.add(parseLine(trimmedLine)); } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) { System.out.println("Skipping invalid saved record on line " + lineNumber + ": " + ex.getMessage());

notes.title: Why the next id is 8 after ids 1 and 7
notes.body:
`loadExpenses` replaces the list and calls `calculateNextId`, which starts at 0, raises it to the highest id in the list, and returns that plus one. With 1 and 7 loaded it returns **8**, and `addExpense` uses it and increments it. Gaps are never filled.

- *Count plus one (3)*: the count is not used.
- *Lowest unused (2)*: no code searches for gaps.
- *Back to 1*: `nextId` starts at 1 only for an empty list; loading recalculates it.

excerpts.quote: if (expense.getId() > highestId) { highestId = expense.getId(); } } return highestId + 1;

notes.title: Why a hand-edited 2.505 crashes the total
notes.body:
The scale rule lives in `parseAmount`, which only typed input goes through. `parseLine` builds the amount with `new BigDecimal(fields.get(2))`, and the `Expense` constructor only checks the sign, so **2.505 loads**. Option 5 then calls `formatAmount`, which uses `setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY)`. Dropping the 5 would change the value, so it throws `ArithmeticException: Rounding necessary`. Nothing catches it; the `finally` block saves, and the program ends with a stack trace.

- *Skipped at load*: load-time parsing never checks the scale.
- *$2.51 or $2.505*: `formatAmount` neither rounds nor prints more than two decimals; it throws.

excerpts.quote: private String formatAmount(BigDecimal amount) { return amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY).toPlainString();

notes.title: Why an expense without a note does not survive a restart
notes.body:
`toLine` always writes six fields, so an empty note leaves a tab at the very end of the line. On the next start, `load` calls `line.trim()` before parsing, and `trim()` removes trailing whitespace, including that tab. Splitting what is left gives **5 fields**, `parseLine` throws "Expected 6 fields but found 5.", and the record is skipped. The save on exit then rewrites the file without it, so it is **lost**. This is a bug: the trim and the trailing empty field do not fit together.

- *Loads with a dash*: the dash is only how a present but blank note is shown.
- *Note set to "null"*: `toLine` writes an empty string, not null.
- *Date read from the note field*: fields are matched by position only after the count check passes.

excerpts.quote: if (fields.size() != 6) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("Expected 6 fields but found " + fields.size() + ".");
